what: A one-motor WeDo rover rolls on one driven wheel and two front ball castors. Its forward-looking distance sensor can stop it before a wall. Distance feedback stops a one-motor rover.
try: Reset and load the rover example on its wall mat. Predict where it will stop.
Run and watch the distance reading decrease as the driven wheel moves the chassis.
Reset, use a low manual motor setting, then Stop. Compare manual stopping with the sensor-controlled program.
why: The distance sensor provides feedback about the environment. The program stops the drive when its condition is met; fixed running time alone would depend on speed and starting position. This WeDo motor has no encoder, so it cannot provide a measured shaft-position hold.
matters: Obstacle detection links a sensor condition to a physical action.
question: If the rover starts farther from the wall, should a distance-triggered program need a longer drive time?
answer: Yes, it travels farther before reaching the same sensor condition. A fixed-time program would instead stop after the same duration, at a different distance.
further: Compare with the two-motor wall stopper and its distance reading.
Identify which port drives the motor and which carries the distance sensor.
